subtasks.name: Receive and sort claim documents
subtasks.description: Intake staff receive the receipts and other documents sent by claimants and sort them by type (treatment, medication, travel). The model would classify each document.
subtasks.rationale: Sorting follows clear categories and mistakes are usually caught at later steps, so rework is minor. Documents belong to identifiable claimants.

subtasks.name: Extract receipt fields with source text
subtasks.description: Read each receipt and pull out amounts, dates and other fields, keeping the matching source text so staff can verify each value.
subtasks.rationale: Field capture is rule-based and the source text lets errors be caught before the decision. A wrong amount causes rework or delay.

subtasks.name: Key in amounts and dates
subtasks.description: Staff enter or confirm the extracted amounts and dates in the claim record so the file is ready for checking against the coverage rules.
subtasks.rationale: Routine data entry with clear steps. Errors are mostly caught in the review that follows, so this step is not itself a decision.

subtasks.name: Validate expenses against coverage rules
subtasks.description: Check each expense against the insurer's coverage rules, for example whether the expense type, date and amount fit what is covered after a collision.
subtasks.rationale: Rules can be written down, but some expenses need interpretation. The result feeds the eligibility recommendation, and an error would change what a claimant is paid.

subtasks.name: Recommend reimbursement eligibility
subtasks.description: Produce a recommendation on whether each expense is eligible for reimbursement, with the reasons, and pass it to the adjuster.
subtasks.rationale: The recommendation directly shapes a benefits decision. Borderline cases need experienced judgment, and a wrong output harms the claimant's money or trust.

subtasks.name: Decide on the claim and write to claimant
subtasks.description: The adjuster reviews the recommendation, decides the claim and writes to the claimant to explain the outcome.
subtasks.rationale: This is the final benefits decision with a significant effect on the claimant. It weighs competing factors and includes communicating the outcome.

assumptions: The adjuster remains the final decision-maker and the model only recommends.
Receipts arrive as scanned images or PDFs that the model can read.
Coverage rules are written down and available for the model to use.
Claim volume is high because the insurer is public and serves many claimants.
Staff still review extracted fields before the recommendation goes to the adjuster.
clarifyingQuestions: Do adjusters see the model's reasons and the source text, or only the recommendation?
How are unclear or unreadable receipts handled today?
Which coverage rules need interpretation rather than a simple check?

narrative.executiveSummary: Verdict: go with conditions, at the AIA-inspired indicative tier II. The case likely triggers BC FIPPA requirements on a privacy impact assessment, reasonable security and storage outside Canada, and the BC Human Rights Code on algorithmic decisions about people; Splitline rates each an action to complete before a pilot. The privacy office, with the product owner, is the likely owner of the FIPPA items, and the product owner with legal counsel for the Human Rights Code item.
narrative.splitNarrative: AI does it (spot-checked): Receive and sort claim documents, and Extract receipt fields with source text. AI drafts, a person checks and signs off: Validate expenses against coverage rules, Recommend reimbursement eligibility, and Decide on the claim and write to claimant. This is a starting split that the team will move as evidence comes in. The next split review is on 2026-12-26, then monthly.
leverNarratives: Let the team that does the work decide which steps the AI does, and change that over time. Keep this guardrail in place: Shared platform: common tools, common labels, and visible splits. The direct cost is some automation efficiency: you give up part of the consistency and scale you would get from one split shared by all teams.

Let the team adjust the split as it learns, on a fixed base, and re-check it monthly. Keep this guardrail in place: Standardized base: agreed data formats, handoff points, and escalation thresholds. The direct cost is some automation efficiency: the team spends attention adjusting the split, and outputs vary more above the fixed base.

Hold a weekly joint working session between the AI team and the operating unit. Keep this guardrail in place: Retained differentiation: dedicated time for technical and for domain work. The direct cost is some standalone depth on each side: experts and AI specialists spend time on each other's work.
narrative.rolloutNarrative: Days 1–30, Foundation & guardrails: set up the privacy, security and Human Rights Code conditions, the shared platform and the standardized base, and measure baselines. Days 31–60, Shadow pilot & calibration: run the AI in shadow mode, calibrate escalation thresholds and feed corrections back. Days 61–90, Controlled scale & audit: go live in controlled increments, hold the first split review and audit a sample of decisions. Track three KPIs: Straight-through processing rate; Decision quality on non-routine cases (sampled expert review); Adjuster corrections per 100 claims.
